source: Kraishan (2026) The Long Road to the Same Answer: Cognitive Bias Under Escalating Reasoning Budgets in LLMs (IEEE CogMI 2026)
finding: Reasoning models were not less biased than matched non-reasoning siblings. The point estimate leaned the other way in every family, but the pooled item-level test was not reliable.
numbers: 30 vignettes (5 per bias, six biases, from the Malberg 30,000-test benchmark), 7 models in 4 families (Claude Haiku 4.5 with and without thinking, GPT-5.1 thinking on/off, DeepSeek-R1 vs V3, Qwen3 thinking vs instruct), 10 samples per cell, 12,350 calls. Pooled reasoning minus sibling bias magnitude = +0.031, 95% CI [-0.010, +0.074], t(29)=1.45, p=.157, dz=0.27. Per-family dz 0.08 to 0.26.
quote: reasoning models are not less biased than their siblings
limits: Only 5 items per bias, so item-level tests are weak. DeepSeek and Qwen cannot turn thinking off, so their contrast crosses a sibling boundary (V3, Qwen3-Instruct). Items are from a public benchmark, not fresh. Ordinal choice tasks, not free numeric estimates.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2 (partly): extra thinking tokens do not by themselves remove these biases. Do not rely on thinking mode as the S1 hygiene step.

source: Kraishan (2026) The Long Road to the Same Answer (dose-response, RQ2)
finding: Bias did not fall as the realised number of reasoning tokens grew. Where anything moved, the signed score drifted further from the human direction.
numbers: Requested ceilings 0, 1,024, 4,096, 8,192 tokens; realised tokens logged. Claude realised 0 to about 800 tokens: slope of |s| +0.0029 per doubling, t(29)=0.91, p=.372. DeepSeek-R1 about 700 to 2,800 tokens and Qwen3 about 500 to 3,400 tokens: slopes null (p=.958, p=.213). GPT-5.1 realised only 0 to about 225 tokens; |s| rose (beta +0.0084, p=.018). All six per-bias slope tests null after correction.
quote: no model's susceptibility to the manipulations reliably decreased
limits: Realised deliberation was small for some providers (requested budget is not used budget). The token range is short compared with long-thinking math runs.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: this is the nearest thing to a token-matched test (same weights for Claude and GPT-5.1, thinking toggled). Result: no gain from more thinking on these judgment items. 'Robustness comes from training or input handling, not token count' stays a hypothesis.

source: Kraishan (2026) The Long Road to the Same Answer (presence vs reversal, RQ3)
finding: Across all seven current models, only anchoring pointed in the human direction. Framing, loss aversion, escalation and confirmation leaned the opposite way; availability was absent.
numbers: Mean signed score (85 model-by-budget cells per bias): anchoring +0.163, 95% CI [+0.111,+0.215], d=+1.89, p_Holm=.037 (range +0.11 Qwen3-thinking to +0.20 Claude instruct). Framing -0.336, d=-2.35, p_Holm=.010 (reversed). Loss aversion -0.586 (largest, CI [-0.914,+0.031]). Escalation -0.070. Confirmation -0.139. Availability -0.035, not reliable (absent).
limits: Scores use the Malberg benchmark's own definition, not human effect sizes. Five items per bias. 'Reversed' framing may come from option wording or scale-reversal handling in the benchmark, not a real anti-framing disposition.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 7 (partly): for 2025-26 models, numeric anchoring is the bias that still shows up; framing and availability do not copy the human direction on this benchmark. Put S1 effort on numeric anchors first.

source: Kraishan (2026) The Long Road to the Same Answer (verbalise-the-anchor, RQ4)
finding: One prompt line telling the model to restate every number in the prompt before answering lowered anchoring on all five anchoring items. More thinking did not.
numbers: Pooled change -0.015 in signed score, 95% CI [-0.026,-0.004] over cells; item means -0.004 to -0.036; item-level t(4)=-2.65, p=.057; sign test 5 of 5, p=.063. Five of seven models moved the same way.
limits: Not significant at the item level (p=.057). The effect is small against a mean anchoring score of +0.163 (under 10 percent of it). Restating is not the same as removing the number from the input.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 (partial): a cheap 'name the anchor' step is directional, not proven. No head-to-head against input rewrite or counter-anchoring exists. Test it as one arm.

source: Yao (2026) When the Thinking Mode Strengthens the Anchor: Authority-Rationalized Anchoring in LLM Legal Judgment (SSRN 6975478)
finding: Turning thinking on made 6 of 7 deployed models adopt a credible-looking anchor more, not less. In 3 models the same toggle reduced a low-credibility anchor and raised a high-credibility one.
numbers: 7 models, thinking toggled on/off, Chinese personal-injury damages estimates, anchor attributed to 5 sources from fortune teller to chief judge. Within-model sign reversal graded by source credibility, significant at 30 cases per model and reproduced at 100 cases in a length-matched extension.
quote: Leaving thinking on is not a generic safeguard
limits: Abstract only (read via Crossref); full tables not opened. SSRN preprint, not peer reviewed. Single legal-estimation domain. Authors say downward adoption may be rational source-weighting.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: thinking can reason toward a cited number when the source looks authoritative. Source attribution should be stripped at S1, not left for the thinking step to weigh.

source: Shahriar et al. (2026) Words Speak Louder Than Code: Cognitive Heuristics in LLM-Based Code Vulnerability Detection
finding: Context around identical code (author title, task framing, prior analysis result) flips vulnerability verdicts in all eight models. Telling the model to ignore metadata mostly failed.
numbers: 8 LLMs (LLaMA 4, LLaMA 3, DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, Claude, GPT, Gemini), 3 languages. Mean susceptibility: framing 33.2%, anchoring 23.5%, halo 18.4%. Attack success rate (true positives flipped to SAFE), per model in that order: framing 63.5/76.9/91.9/89.8/50.3/33.0/31.7/25.1; anchoring 42.5/67.4/52.7/28.3/49.4/17.0/10.3/5.9; combined 92.9/97.2/92.6/88.7/74.7/15.8/33.1/45.5. Weak 'ignore metadata' defence on combined: 88.2/87.0/83.1/87.0/64.3/20.9/17.6/27.1. Strong channel-naming defence: 88.5/69.2/49.3/67.8/39.0/24.6/8.9/5.9.
limits: Claude combined ASR got worse under the defences (15.8 to 20.9 to 24.6). Commercial models were more robust than open ones. Single-shot verdicts. Authors only suggest filtering context channels and did not test it.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 5: 'ignore the anchor' prompts fail on context-borne bias in agent code review. The strong version helps on some models only. Supports removing framing channels (PR text, author) before the check.

source: Chergui et al. (2026) Mitigating Anchoring Bias in LLM-Based Agents for Energy-Efficient 6G Autonomous Networks
finding: Small LLM agents negotiating network resources stick to their first proposal. Randomising the starting anchor from a bounded Weibull distribution made them explore.
numbers: One 1B-parameter model (otel-llm-1b-it), temperature 0.1, 200 trials per strategy, up to 5 negotiation rounds, energy saving up to 25% versus the fixed-anchor baseline; mean latency 0.95 s (randomised) vs 1.38 s (fixed).
limits: Simulation, single tiny model, no human baseline, no test against thinking models. The gain is measured against the authors' own fixed heuristic, so it shows rigidity of the agent loop, not a classic H&B estimate.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence for 'randomise the opening anchor of internal proposals' as an agent-loop remedy. Design idea only.

source: Shen et al. (2026) RealICU: Do LLM Agents Understand Long-Context ICU Data?
finding: Across long patient streams, agents kept early interpretations after later contradicting data. Removing the agent's stored insight memory raised accuracy.
numbers: RealICU-Gold 930 windows from 94 MIMIC-IV patients; RealICU-Scale 11,862 windows. Qwen3-235B action recommendation Hit@5 0.526 with insight memory vs 0.601 without. Agent keeps about 6 hypotheses per patient, 80% with anticipatory exceptions. Up to 47.3% of recommendations flagged potentially harmful (recall-safety trade-off). Backbones also Gemini-3.1-pro, GPT-5.4.
limits: 'Anchoring' here is the authors' label for premature commitment in memory-augmented agents; no human anchoring baseline and no controlled irrelevant-number manipulation. LLM hindsight labeler used for the Scale set.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: long context and memory carry the first frame forward. Stored summaries can act as anchors. Our loop should not write unverified conclusions into memory that later steps read as fact.

source: Harshavardhan (2026) Self-Anchoring Calibration Drift in LLMs: How Multi-Turn Conversations Reshape Model Confidence (ACL GEM workshop)
finding: Building on the model's own earlier answers over five turns changed its stated confidence, but differently in each model. The pre-registered 'confidence rises' hypothesis failed.
numbers: Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.2; 15 items per cell; Claude confidence drift -0.032 (t(14)=-2.43, p=.029, d=-0.63; open-ended domain -0.094); GPT-5.2 +0.007 (p=.181); Gemini +0.001. Self-anchoring vs repeated-asking contrast for Claude U=74.5, p=.036. GPT-5.2 ECE change +0.274 in the self-anchored condition vs -0.210 in the control. Drift about zero on factual questions.
limits: Small N, single author, workshop paper. Measures confidence, not numeric estimates. Effects in open-ended domains only.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: multi-turn self-reference moves confidence in model-specific ways, mostly on open-ended tasks. Re-ask from a clean context for calibration checks.

source: Hantel (2026) Small Bias, Large Failure: Anchoring Collapses a Market of Language-Model Agents (SSRN 7095458)
finding: A one-sentence anchor given to seller agents moved a deal price a few dollars alone, but collapsed market efficiency when five cloned sellers all used it. A one-line debiasing instruction reversed the collapse.
numbers: Five-seller market; efficiency fell from 96% to 15% with the anchor given only to sellers; the model that resisted anchoring best one-on-one collapsed the market hardest.
limits: Abstract only (Crossref). Preprint, single market design. Cloned agents share the same bias, so this is the correlated-error case.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: several copies of one model do not cancel a shared anchor, they add up. Critique or debate steps need different framings or inputs, not clones. Pairwise tests can clear a risky model.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators
finding: Swapping the order of two answers changes the verdict a lot. Averaging over both orders and asking for evidence first improved agreement with human judges.
numbers: 80 Vicuna-benchmark questions. Conflict rate when order swapped: GPT-4 46.3% and 5.0% (two comparisons), ChatGPT 82.5% and 52.5%. Vicuna-13B beats ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries by order alone. GPT-4 favours first position, ChatGPT second. Evidence-first plus order-balanced scoring raised accuracy against human labels by 9.8% (GPT-4) and 14.3% (ChatGPT).
limits: 2023 models (GPT-4, ChatGPT). Balanced position doubles the calls, so it is not equal-token. Conflict rate falls as the score gap between answers grows.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: the bias exists in judges. Order balancing works but costs 2x calls. Use it only on close calls (small score gap), not on every check.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
finding: LLM judges show position bias, verbosity bias and possible self-enhancement. Swapping positions and declaring a win only when it holds in both orders is the recommended fix.
numbers: Consistency under position swap (default prompt): Claude-v1 23.8%, GPT-3.5 46.2%, GPT-4 65.0%. Biased toward first: 75.0%, 50.0%, 30.0%. 'Repetitive list' verbosity attack failure rate: Claude-v1 91.3%, GPT-3.5 91.3%, GPT-4 8.7%. Self-enhancement: GPT-4 favours itself with a 10% higher win rate, Claude-v1 25%, GPT-3.5 not.
limits: Authors say the self-enhancement data are too few to settle it. Models from 2023. The conservative swap fix costs two calls per judgement; random assignment is the cheaper alternative they mention.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: same-model self-checking is the case with the least evidence. Random order is a no-token fix for large batches; swap needs 2x tokens.

source: Ye et al. (2024) Justice or Prejudice? Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge (CALM)
finding: Twelve biases measured in six judge models. Position bias gets worse with more answer options. Models rate their own outputs higher even when anonymised.
numbers: 12 bias types; with 3 or 4 candidates most judge models had robustness rate below 0.5 for position bias. Robustness Rate = share of decisions unchanged after injecting the bias. Claude-3.5 was the most robust overall. Authors advise randomising answer order and not using the same model to generate and judge.
limits: Biased variants are made by GPT-4o rewrites, so rewrite quality limits the test. Exact per-model values are in figures and were not all read.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: for a many-candidate verifier (best-of-N), random order is needed and judge and generator should differ if possible.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2 (pdftotext of the full PDF; framing and incidental-anchor rows)
finding: The T&K 1981 framing item replicated at under half the original size. The incidental-anchor effect did not replicate. Note: the ML2 framing item is Study 10 (cheap vs costly item, $5 off), not the Asian disease problem.
numbers: Framing (T&K 1981 Study 10): original d=1.08, 95% CI [0.71,1.45]; replication d=0.40 [0.35,0.45]. Original N=181 (93 vs 88). Incidental anchors (Critcher & Gilovich 2008): original d=0.30 [0.02,0.58]; replication d=0.04 [-0.01,0.09], N about 6,900.
limits: Replication was online; amounts and items updated for 2014. The Asian disease risky-choice problem (T&K 1981) was not in this item.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: corrects the pairing in claim K04: Asian disease primary numbers are still unverified; the primary-read framing effect size is the mental-accounting item (d 1.08 to 0.40).

source: Stegmueller, Binder & Krauss (2024) How general is the natural frequency effect? The case of joint probabilities (Front. Psychol.)
finding: The review part says the evidence that natural frequencies help with joint probabilities and the Linda problem is mixed. The new experiment found no overall natural-frequency advantage for joint probabilities, and the format effect depended on the diagram type.
numbers: 2x5x2 design (probability vs natural frequency; 5 visualisations; mammography vs economics context); the advantage held for double tree diagrams but reversed for 2x2 tables. Review: Fiedler (1988) found better Linda performance with a frequency question; Wedell & Moro (2007) found no systematic difference across several conjunction scenarios.
limits: Secondary on Linda (Fiedler and Wedell & Moro are read through the review). Sample size not extracted. The experiment is on Bayesian joint probabilities, not on Linda itself.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: the 'frequency format cuts Linda errors to 20%' claim (K05) should stay contested. A frequency re-expression is worth trying as an S1 reframe but has no reliable effect size.

source: Mayer & Rebholz (2024) Navigating Anchor Relevance Skillfully: Expertise Reduces Susceptibility to Anchoring Effects (PsyArXiv)
finding: In two preregistered experiments, experts anchored less than novices and more extreme anchors anchored more. Anchor relevance had no effect.
limits: Abstract only (Crossref); effect sizes and N not extracted. Perceptual estimation task. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a human moderator design that can be run on LLMs: expertise (domain knowledge in the prompt), anchor extremity, relevance. Prediction: extremity matters; relevance may not.

source: Lou & Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study (full text re-read for moderators)
finding: Only 11 of 162 anchor-minus-control differences went against the hint direction. Stronger models were more consistently anchored. Time-period answers were the hardest to anchor.
numbers: 42 questions, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o, 30 answers per treatment at temperature 0.8, t-tests. 11 exceptions of 162 values; 9 of the 11 from GPT-3.5. Time-period questions were 7 of 42 (17%) but 6 of the 11 exceptions (54%). In 78 of 108 GPT-4/4o experiments the 30 answers were identical (std about 0). Irrelevant first hint (8 cases) gave large answer variance, not blind copying.
limits: Models are 2023-24; no reasoning models; no anchor-distance sweep. Zero variance in many cells makes t-tests fragile.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: answer type (dates vs quantities) and model strength both predict LLM anchoring; relevance and distance were not varied. A real moderator sweep is still to do.

source: Ryu, Kim & Kim (2024) A Study on the Representativeness Heuristics Problem in LLMs (IEEE Access); Li & Rui (2024) Are LLMs Immune to Representativeness Bias? (SSRN 4976447)
finding: Two papers on LLM representativeness were found by title in Crossref. Full text and abstracts could not be opened (IEEE returned 418; SSRN gave no abstract).
limits: Not read. Do not cite results.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open: no opened source gives base-rate or sample-size error rates for current models on rewritten items.

source: Nawaz (2026) Reframing Anchoring Bias Measurement: A Logistic Regression Approach to Anchor Proximity (PsyArXiv)
finding: Whether anchoring is 'detected' depends on how it is scored. With a categorical within-50%-of-anchor rule, neither anchor value nor confidence predicted who anchored.
limits: Abstract only; small human study; preprint. Does not contradict the aggregate effect.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: choose the scoring rule before running agent tests (directional gap between low and high anchor arms, not proximity), and report both.
